subject: history
subtitle: The Act of Union creating Great Britain, Jacobite rebellions, and the formation of British identity.

data.targetWord: the law that joined the Kingdom of England (including Wales) and the Kingdom of Scotland into one new state called the Kingdom of Great Britain, with a single Parliament at Westminster

examples.en-GB: The Act of Union 1707 ended Scotland's separate Parliament but protected its legal system and Presbyterian church.

data.targetWord: the new state created by the Act of Union in 1707, formed by the union of England (including Wales) and Scotland; Ireland was not included

examples.en-GB: The Kingdom of Great Britain was created in 1707 — it did not include Ireland, which joined only in 1801 to form the United Kingdom.

data.targetWord: the moment in 1603 when James VI of Scotland became James I of England and Ireland, meaning one person ruled both kingdoms, though they remained separate states with separate Parliaments

examples.en-GB: The Union of the Crowns in 1603 shared a monarch between England and Scotland but did not create one country.

data.targetWord: a failed Scottish attempt in the 1690s to establish a colony in Panama that collapsed due to disease, poor planning, Spanish opposition and lack of English support, leaving many Scottish investors bankrupt

examples.en-GB: The failure of the Darien Scheme weakened Scotland's economy and made union with England seem more attractive to some Scottish politicians.

data.targetWord: a supporter of the deposed Stuart king James II and VII or his descendants, who believed the Stuarts had a rightful hereditary claim to the British throne

examples.en-GB: Jacobites opposed the Hanoverian succession and wanted to restore the Stuart dynasty to the throne of Great Britain.

data.targetWord: linked to the royal family from Hanover in Germany, beginning with George I in 1714, who inherited the British throne because Parliament wanted a Protestant successor

examples.en-GB: George I was the first Hanoverian king and his succession angered Jacobites who supported the Stuart claim.

data.targetWord: the Jacobite prince who led the 1745 rising, known to supporters as Bonnie Prince Charlie, who invaded from Scotland and marched into England before his army retreated and was defeated at Culloden

examples.en-GB: Charles Edward Stuart raised his standard at Glenfinnan in 1745 and led the last major Jacobite attempt to reclaim the British throne.

data.targetWord: the battle of 16 April 1746 in which the Duke of Cumberland's government forces defeated the Jacobite army under Charles Edward Stuart, ending the last major Jacobite rising

examples.en-GB: The Battle of Culloden ended the last Jacobite challenge to the Hanoverian throne and was followed by the government targeting Highland clan power.

data.targetWord: the order in which people inherit the throne; the question of Protestant versus Catholic succession was central to both the Act of Union and the Jacobite risings

examples.en-GB: England passed the Act of Settlement in 1701 to secure Protestant succession, which contributed to pressure for union with Scotland.

data.targetWord: a Highland kinship and loyalty group often linked to a chief, family name and ancestral land, which formed the basis of military and social organisation in the Scottish Highlands

examples.en-GB: Some Highland clans supported Jacobitism due to local loyalties, rivalries or hopes for advantage, though not all Highlanders were Jacobites.

data.targetWord: the power to govern independently; many opponents of the Act of Union argued that it destroyed Scottish sovereignty by ending the Scottish Parliament

examples.en-GB: Critics of the Act of Union argued that sovereignty could not be bought or bargained away, and that Scotland had lost its independence.

data.targetWord: a law passed after Culloden in 1746 that reduced the traditional legal powers of Highland clan chiefs, weakening their authority over their people

examples.en-GB: The Heritable Jurisdictions Act was one of several measures the government used after Culloden to break the power of Highland clan chiefs.

data.targetWord: an organised attempt to resist or overthrow an established government or ruler; the Jacobite risings of 1715 and 1745 were attempts to overthrow the Hanoverian monarchy

examples.en-GB: The 1745 Jacobite rebellion was the most dramatic challenge to the Hanoverian state, reaching as far south as Derby.

data.targetWord: an English law threatening to treat Scottish people as aliens and restrict Scottish trade with England unless Scotland accepted negotiations about succession and union, putting economic pressure on Scotland

examples.en-GB: The Alien Act 1705 showed that England could use economic pressure to force Scotland into union negotiations.

data.targetWord: a law passed after Culloden restricting many Highlanders from wearing traditional Highland dress, including the tartan kilt, as part of the government's attempt to suppress Jacobite culture

examples.en-GB: The Dress Act was one of the government's attempts after Culloden to remove the symbols of Highland identity associated with the Jacobite cause.

data.targetWord: the battle in September 1745 in which Jacobite forces under Charles Edward Stuart defeated a government army near Edinburgh, showing the Jacobites could be a serious military threat

examples.en-GB: The Jacobite victory at Prestonpans gave Charles Edward Stuart control of Edinburgh and seemed to show the rising could succeed.

data.targetWord: a form of Protestant Christianity organised without bishops, with each congregation having equal authority; the Church of Scotland was Presbyterian and its protection was guaranteed by the Act of Union

examples.en-GB: Scottish Presbyterians were concerned that union might threaten their church, but the Act of Union promised to protect the Presbyterian Church of Scotland.

data.targetWord: the British government commander who defeated the Jacobites at the Battle of Culloden in 1746; he became known as 'Butcher Cumberland' because of the harsh treatment of Jacobites after the battle

examples.en-GB: The Duke of Cumberland commanded the government forces that defeated Charles Edward Stuart's Jacobite army at Culloden.

data.targetWord: a person or group's sense of who they are, which can include national, religious, regional, family and cultural aspects; after 1707, people could hold multiple identities such as Scottish and British simultaneously

examples.en-GB: The Act of Union encouraged a British identity to develop alongside existing Scottish, Welsh, English and Irish identities.

data.targetWord: the son of James II and VII and the Jacobite claimant to the throne, known by supporters as James III and VIII, and by opponents as the Old Pretender; he led the 1715 Jacobite rising

examples.en-GB: James Francis Edward Stuart, the Old Pretender, arrived in Scotland too late to help the failing 1715 rising.

data.targetWord: money paid to Scotland as part of the 1707 union settlement, partly to compensate investors who had lost money in the Darien Scheme and to balance the financial arrangements of union

examples.en-GB: The Equivalent was a financial payment to Scotland to help compensate for Darien losses and was part of the political bargaining that made union possible.

data.targetWord: the historical alliance between Scotland and France that had existed for centuries; fear that an independent Scotland might revive this alliance and threaten England from the north was one English reason for wanting union in 1707

examples.en-GB: English politicians feared that without union, Scotland might use the Auld Alliance with France as a bargaining tool against England.

data.targetWord: the English law that determined the Protestant Hanoverian line of succession after Queen Anne, and which alarmed some Scottish politicians who felt it ignored Scotland's right to choose its own monarch

examples.en-GB: The Act of Settlement 1701 showed that the English Parliament was deciding the future monarchy without consulting Scotland.

data.targetWord: laws passed after Culloden restricting the possession of weapons in the Highlands, intended to prevent future Jacobite rebellions by reducing the military capacity of Highland clans

examples.en-GB: The Disarming Acts after Culloden were part of the government's effort to prevent Highland clans from raising private armies again.

data.targetWord: the state formed in 1801 when Great Britain united with Ireland to become the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland; this is different from Great Britain created in 1707, which did not include Ireland

examples.en-GB: The United Kingdom was created in 1801, not 1707; the 1707 Act of Union only created Great Britain, which did not include Ireland.

Jacobites should not be confused with ____, who were a political group in the French Revolution.

data.title: Put the key events in the history of Union and the Jacobite risings in chronological order
items: James VI of Scotland becomes James I of England (Union of the Crowns, 1603)
Darien Scheme fails, weakening Scotland's economy (1698–1700)
English Act of Settlement determines Protestant Hanoverian succession (1701)
Act of Union creates Kingdom of Great Britain (1707)
George I becomes first Hanoverian king (1714)
First Jacobite rising under the Earl of Mar (1715)
Charles Edward Stuart lands in Scotland and wins at Prestonpans (1745)
Battle of Culloden ends the last Jacobite rising (1746)

data.title: Order the consequences of Culloden for Highland society from most immediate to most far-reaching
items: Executions and punishments for Jacobite leaders
Confiscation of rebel estates
Disarming Acts restrict weapons in the Highlands
Dress Act restricts Highland dress including tartan
Heritable Jurisdictions Act reduces clan chiefs' legal powers
Military roads and forts built to control the region
Jacobitism becomes impractical as a military cause

data.title: Order the events of the 1745 Jacobite rising
items: Charles Edward Stuart lands in the Hebrides
Charles raises his standard at Glenfinnan and gains Highland support
Jacobites capture Edinburgh
Jacobites win the Battle of Prestonpans (September 1745)
Jacobite army marches into England and reaches Derby (December 1745)
Jacobites retreat to Scotland
Jacobites win at Falkirk but fail to press advantage (January 1746)
Government forces defeat Jacobites at Culloden (April 1746)
